clinicalPearls: Benign but locally aggressive primary bone neoplasm that typically arises in the skeletally mature young adult.
Characteristically located in the epiphysis of long bones extending to the subchondral plate, most often around the knee (distal femur and proximal tibia), the distal radius and the sacrum.
Composed of neoplastic mononuclear stromal cells together with abundant reactive osteoclast-like multinucleated giant cells.
Driven by a recurrent H3F3A (histone H3.3) G34W mutation in the stromal cells, detectable by mutation-specific immunohistochemistry and useful diagnostically.
Stromal cells over-express RANKL, recruiting and activating the osteoclast-like giant cells that resorb bone — the rationale for denosumab therapy.
Radiographs show an eccentric, expansile, purely lytic lesion with a non-sclerotic margin and no matrix mineralisation.
Standard treatment is intralesional curettage with local adjuvants and cavity filling; denosumab is used for unresectable, axial or sacral disease and to downstage before surgery.
Rarely, histologically benign tumours seed indolent pulmonary deposits, and malignant transformation may occur, particularly after radiotherapy.
reference.pathophysiology: Giant cell tumour of bone is a neoplasm in which the proliferating, mutated component is the mononuclear stromal cell, while the striking multinucleated giant cells that give the lesion its name are reactive, non-neoplastic osteoclasts recruited into the tumour. The great majority of stromal cells carry a driver mutation in the H3F3A gene encoding histone H3.3, most commonly the G34W substitution, which alters chromatin regulation and can be highlighted with a mutation-specific antibody. These stromal cells secrete receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL), which binds RANK on monocyte precursors and drives their fusion into osteoclast-like giant cells; the resulting intense osteoclastic resorption produces the expansile, lytic lesion seen radiologically and provides the therapeutic rationale for the RANKL-blocking antibody denosumab. The tumour favours the epiphysis of long bones in the mature skeleton and, although classified as benign, behaves locally aggressively, breaching cortex and occasionally producing histologically bland pulmonary implants. Secondary aneurysmal bone cyst change is common, and true malignant transformation, though rare, is a recognised late event, especially after irradiation.
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs of the affected bone, which are often characteristic
MRI to assess soft tissue extension and joint involvement
CT to evaluate cortical integrity and matrix
Biopsy with histopathology and H3.3 G34W mutation-specific immunohistochemistry
CT of the chest to exclude pulmonary deposits
Serum calcium and parathyroid hormone to exclude a brown tumour
redFlags: Cortical breach with a soft tissue mass or rapid enlargement
Axial, spinal or sacral disease with neurological compromise
New pain or destructive change after radiotherapy, suggesting malignant transformation
reference.prognosis: The overall prognosis is good, but local recurrence after curettage is well recognised, particularly at the distal radius. Pulmonary deposits are uncommon and often indolent, denosumab controls otherwise unresectable disease, and the rare malignant transformation carries a markedly worse outlook.
pitfalls: Assuming benign histology excludes the possibility of pulmonary deposits
Misinterpreting denosumab-induced new bone formation, which can obscure the diagnosis, and forgetting the risk of rebound growth after the drug is stopped
Overlooking a secondary aneurysmal bone cyst component
Failing to check calcium and parathyroid hormone and thereby confusing the lesion with a brown tumour of hyperparathyroidism
Using radiotherapy without recognising the associated risk of malignant transformation
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone
management: Surgical resection of the lesion is the primary treatment for resectable disease.
Choice between intralesional curettage with adjuvant and cavity filling versus wider en-bloc resection is standard orthopaedic-oncology decision making.
Denosumab, a RANK ligand inhibiting monoclonal antibody, is approved for tumours that are surgically unsalvageable or where resection would cause severe morbidity.
Denosumab can be used as definitive therapy when surgery is not feasible, such as unresectable or axial or sacral disease.
Denosumab can also be used pre-operatively to downstage a tumour so a more limited surgical procedure can be attempted.
Denosumab discontinuation has been associated with a higher rate of local recurrence, so patients who stop therapy warrant closer surveillance.
Long term safety, optimal maintenance frequency, and overall therapeutic strategy for denosumab in this disease remain open questions.
Radiographic follow up for local recurrence is standard after definitive local treatment, with added vigilance at higher risk sites.
Longitudinal follow up should include screening for pulmonary deposits and surveillance for rare malignant transformation.
Any new, suspected, or biopsy proven case should be referred to an orthopaedic oncology multidisciplinary team before definitive treatment planning.
Axial, sacral, or otherwise surgically unsalvageable tumours, or those where resection carries high risk of severe functional morbidity, should prompt multidisciplinary consideration of denosumab.

New or progressive pain, radiographic change after prior radiotherapy, or atypical or aggressive lesion features should raise concern for malignant transformation and prompt urgent oncology re-referral.
